72	Applying RATE's Likert ATE methodology \citep{reber2025rate} to our formality style-transformed pairs yields Cohen's $d = 0.10$, $p = 0.33$ (non-significant, $n = 88$); pairwise comparison on identical data reveals a 63.0\% formal preference ($p = 0.0004$, Bradley-Terry on all 173 comparisons), confirmed by a consistency-filtered sign test (73.9\%, $p = 0.006$, $n = 46$ consistent pairs).
73	This is the Likert Blindspot: the same data, the same style intervention, two measurement instruments---one detects bias, the other does not.
74	A $4\times$ scaled replication ($n = 355$) distinguishes measurement attenuation from insufficient power: the Likert effect size shrinks to $d = {-}0.039$ (near zero) while BT remains stable at $67.5\%$ ($p < 0.0001$)---if the gap were merely statistical power, $d$ would remain non-zero at larger $n$.

\section*{Limitations}
\label{sec:limitations}

\paragraph{Quality--style confounding and construct validity.}
The NLI gate blocks content changes but cannot block quality perception shifts mediated by style itself---a fundamental identifiability limit of text-rewriting approaches.
Although the formality effect survives logistic adjustment for original preference ($\text{OR} = 2.32$, $p = 0.006$; Appendix~\ref{app:direction}), residual confounding is not fully eliminated.
An alternative interpretation of the Blindspot is that Likert and pairwise modes measure different constructs: Likert captures absolute quality difference while pairwise captures ordinal preference. Under this view, the divergence reflects construct difference rather than measurement failure, with different practical implications for audit design (\S\ref{sec:likert_pairwise}).
This example reflects a consistent pattern: surface-level style features alone explain most of the variance in judge scores \citep{murugadoss2025sos}, with 76--92\% of preferences originating from style cues \citep{li2026preference,soumik2026judging}.
The primary open question is whether pairwise comparison detects genuine style bias or amplifies micro-preferences inherent in the format. Definitive resolution requires human evaluation comparing Likert and pairwise judgments on identical pairs---an important direction for future work.
While our controls bound the amplification factor, we cannot quantify it precisely without a ground-truth bias magnitude---an inherent limitation of observational-format comparisons.

\paragraph{Evaluator-producer bias and generalizability.}
Qwen3-32B serves as both rewriter and judge, raising self-preference concerns \citep{panickssery2024selfpreference}; an independent GPT-4o rewriter bounds this to a 22\% Style OR reduction (Appendix~\ref{app:rewriter_indep}).
This 22\% represents a lower bound: all alternative rewriters are instruction-tuned LLMs that may share style preferences acquired during RLHF training, leaving open the possibility that a human or rule-based rewriter would yield larger reductions.
GPT-4o, Llama-3.3-70B, and Gemini-2.5-Flash use a separate rewriter and are not subject to evaluator-producer overlap; all three independently confirm the Blindspot across four architectures, though cross-judge effect-size comparisons are not valid.
Cross-rewriter validation shows that Blindspot existence is robust to rewriter identity, but effect-size precision varies by approximately ${\pm}22\%$ with rewriter choice (Appendix~\ref{app:rewriter_indep}).
Register results carry the highest evaluator-producer risk---all register rewrites use the same Qwen3-32B rewriter without the cross-rewriter validation applied to formality and verbosity---and register conclusions remain tentative pending independent rewriter validation.
Claude Sonnet~4's formality style sensitivity is consistently low across all three benchmarks (GEE Style OR $1.47$--$1.99$, all n.s.; Appendix~\ref{app:claude_crossbench}); its elevated aggregate BT on AEval/MT-Bench ($70$--$73\%$) reflects quality detection (Orig OR $9$--$12$) rather than style preference.
Verbosity sensitivity is benchmark-dependent (AEval Style OR $= 4.76$, $p < .001$; LLMBar n.s.), confirming that style bias is a judge$\times$benchmark$\times$axis interaction rather than a fixed judge property.
\paragraph{Scope and ecological validity.}
CSD is currently applicable to surface-level stylistic attributes (formality, verbosity, register) whose rewrites preserve semantic content.
Semantic-level axes---hedging, humor, technicality---inherently alter meaning during rewriting, causing the NLI gate to systematically reject valid style variants.
A tone axis pilot (assertive $\to$ hedging) confirmed this boundary: the NLI gate correctly rejected 55\% of rewrites because epistemic commitment changes violate content equivalence, bounding CSD's current applicability to surface-level axes.
Primary analyses use LLMBar ($n = 100$); additional axes, larger benchmarks, and further judges are needed.
Our per-axis decomposition treats each style axis independently; in practice, axes may interact (e.g., formality shifts may co-vary with register), and such confounds are not isolated by the current design.
Cross-axis contamination analysis (Appendix~\ref{app:cross_axis_contamination}) confirms that formality rewrites produce negligible changes in sentence structure ($|d| < 0.03$) and verbosity rewrites leave lexical diversity unchanged (TTR $|d| < 0.04$).
Our empirical evidence covers three style axes (formality, verbosity, register); whether the per-axis confound taxonomy generalizes to other axes (e.g., hedging level, bullet-point vs.\ prose) remains open.
Our controlled manipulation design ensures internal validity but may not fully generalize to naturalistic evaluation settings where style and content covary.

\paragraph{Validation methodology and scale design.}
NLI validation uses Qwen3-32B as annotator (GPT-4o cross-validation on all 200 pairs confirms 92.1\% formality / 82.6\% verbosity pass precision); two independent annotators confirm $98.6\%$ pass precision on 100 pairs ($69/70$ gate-passed; AC$_1 = 0.96$; \S\ref{sec:nli_validation}).
A 100-point continuous scale does not resolve the Blindspot across three judges (Appendix~\ref{app:likert100}), suggesting the gap reflects measurement mode rather than granularity \citep{preston2000scale}.
The Bradley-Terry model assumes unidimensionality---a single latent ``quality'' dimension---which is standard in evaluation contexts but not empirically verified here; if judges evaluate along multiple latent dimensions, BT estimates may conflate distinct preference axes.
Per-axis TOST at $\Delta = 10$pp is underpowered (power ${\approx}42\%$); pooled TOST ($n = 174$) achieves equivalence at $\Delta = 12$pp ($p = .035$) but not at $\Delta = 10$pp.
Claude's near-null LLMBar profile rests on convergent evidence (TOST, cross-benchmark GEE consistency, the GPT-4o contrast, and Bayesian equivalence testing) rather than formal equivalence alone.
Equivalence testing \citep{lakens2017equivalence} with larger samples could formalize whether the Likert effect size is practically zero.
